rules_text:
Rules summary Contents 1 Objective 2 Setup 3 Game play 3.1 Placement Phase 3.2 Resolution Phase 4 Game End 5 Abilities of Influences Objective In Oriflamme (Citadels 2), players play for 6 rounds by playing influence cards and activating them. To seize power, you must conspire, fight and deduce how others will play. The player with the highest influence after 6 rounds wins! Setup Each player takes 10 cards of their colour and removes 3 randomly. Everyone starts with 1 influence. The resolution direction is placed. Game play Each round consists of 2 phases. After the phases are played, the first player tile is passed to the left. Placement Phase The first player chooses a card and places it face down in the middle of the table. The next player places another card to the left or right of all cards already placed. You cannot play between cards. Starting from the second round, you may place a card on top of your own card already in play. While a card is underneath another card, it cannot be targeted or revealed. It cannot gain influence or use its ability. Once everyone has played a card, the placement phase is over. Resolution Phase Starting from the first card, players choose whether to reveal them. If the card is not revealed, 1 influence is placed on it. If the card is revealed, apply the card's effect and take all influences on it. Repeat until the end of the queue is reached. Each time you eliminate a card, you get 1 influence. Cards in the queue will remain until they are discarded or eliminated. Cards in the same family can be stacked. However, a covered card can never be revealed or targeted. Game End The game ends when 6 rounds are played. Influences still on the cards do not count. The player with the most influence wins. In case of a tie, the tied player with the most cards in the influence queue wins. Abilities of Influences Ambush : If revealed by another card, discard that card and gain 4 influence, otherwise, gain 1 influence and discard ambush with any influence on it. Archer : Eliminate the first or last card from the queue. Assassination : Eliminate any card in the queue. Discard assassination. Conspiracy : Gain double the amount of influence on the card. Discard conspiracy. Heir : If there are no other cards revealed with the same name, gain 2 influence. Lord : Earn 1 influence, plus 1 influence per adjacent card in your family. Royal Decree : Move a card wherever you want in the queue. Discard royal decree. Shapeshifter : Copy the ability (not the name) of an adjacent card. Soldier : Eliminate an adjacent card. Spy : Steal 1 influence from a player with a card adjacent to the spy.

[Rating: 2/10] Didn't do enough to grab me over other short-card-game candidates for a game night starter/dessert.  Reminds me of Citadels for some reason: although you play the cards into a row and trigger them more deliberately against your neighbours here, I think it has some of the same vibe and a need to get familiar with and second-guess others' use of the various cards available.

[Rating: 3/10] This game is pure chaos. Man told me it is call "bluff" but how could you actually guess anything when you have no clue of what your opponents have in hand (they are randomly discarding 3 cards out of 10 at the beginning of the game). Otherwise, arts work, the rounds are quick and the game is easy to get in. But this is not sufficient to turn it into a good game. Basically, I am asking every player I meet who played this game "did you do a nice shot" and none could answer me "yes" without mentionning luck or good fortune. [Rating: 3/10] I like a game like Campy Creature more for bluffing. This was a fun experience, but I think it can be hard on some players more than it provides them fun.

[Rating: 3.5/10] Simple rules, but not very elegant. There are some decisions, but the result is mostly random, depending on what the others do. They can even target you specifically. A bit too long. The kind of game I would play once with friends for a laugh and then forget about it until the next decade.

[Rating: 3.5/10] I was hyped about an easy to learn and confrontative game. Rewarded in France as best game. But it is mechanically pretty bad. There are way to less trap cards, and defensive play is not possible. Only the beautiful art design by the polish artist Tomek Jedruszek deceives about a bad game.

[Rating: 3.5/10] Oriflamme is a bit boring. Cards have more or less obvious use cases that get muddied in the butterfly effect of their resolution order.
